summary: Gives an applicability statement for using GMPLS protocols to support Basic Mode Layer 1 VPNs. In Basic Mode, no routing information is exchanged between the Layer 1 network and the customer. It examines how GMPLS protocols can meet the requirements. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This paper checks whether an existing set of tools is a good fit for private shared fiber links, and how to use it.

questions: how does gmpls control optical circuits
what is the difference between customer and provider control
what information does the provider share with customers
subtitle: How GMPLS can support Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks

tldr.problem: Service providers need to offer Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks (L1VPNs) that partition fiber links and optical circuits among multiple customers. Applicability of existing GMPLS protocols for this use case needs to be defined.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how GMPLS signaling and control mechanisms (particularly RFC 5251) can be used to set up and manage L1VPN Basic Mode networks, where routing information is not exchanged between the provider and customer domains.
tldr.outcome: GMPLS provides the signaling and resource management needed for Basic Mode L1VPNs, enabling service providers to offer optical circuit services with customer-controlled topology but provider-controlled infrastructure.

today: RFC 5253 is Informational and defines the applicability of GMPLS to L1VPN Basic Mode. It remains the authoritative statement of how GMPLS techniques map to Basic Mode L1VPN requirements. Enhanced Mode L1VPNs, which do exchange routing information, are addressed in separate documents.

sections.title: L1VPN and Basic Mode
sections.content:
A Layer 1 Virtual Private Network (L1VPN) allows a service provider to partition its fiber infrastructure into separate virtual networks for different customers. Each customer rents L1VPN connections—optical circuits or time-division multiplexed (TDM) channels—between their sites.

The Basic Mode of L1VPN operation is the simpler of two models: the provider controls and manages all routing within its network, while the customer controls only which sites connect to which other sites. Critically, the customer and provider networks do not exchange routing information. This provides strong separation and topology confidentiality but requires the provider to manage all path computation and resource allocation.
sections.eli5: A provider offers to connect a customer's offices with optical fiber. The customer decides which offices should talk to which. The provider decides the actual path the light travels and handles all the technical details. They do not share route information with each other.

sections.title: GMPLS Suitability and Control Plane
sections.content:
GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) extends MPLS to control all switching layers, not just packet switching. It uses RSVP-TE signaling to establish label-switched paths (LSPs) across optical networks. RFC 5251 extends GMPLS signaling to support L1VPN connections between customer edge (CE) equipment and provider edge (PE) equipment.

In Basic Mode, the provider network is controlled by GMPLS within a single autonomous system (AS). The PE and CE communicate over a control channel that must remain reachable at the IP level. When a customer requests a connection between two sites, the CE sends a signaling message to its PE, which computes a path across the provider network and reserves optical resources. The GMPLS control plane handles all path computation, label allocation, and resource management on the provider's behalf.
sections.eli5: GMPLS is a set of rules for telling optical switches where to send light. The provider uses GMPLS to handle all the switching decisions inside its network. The customer just sends a message saying 'connect my two offices' and the provider's GMPLS system figures out the rest.

sections.title: Network Types and Provisioning
sections.content:
The RFC covers how GMPLS supports various data plane technologies. Provider networks can consist of time-division multiplexed (TDM) switches, optical cross-connects (OXCs), or photonic cross-connects (PXCs). A PE can be a standalone device or an Ethernet Private Line (EPL) adapter that maps Ethernet frames onto Layer 1 circuits. Provider networks may offer single switching granularities (e.g., only VC3/VC4 channels) or multiple granularities, and single or multiple connection types.

Provisioning of L1VPN connectivity requires maintaining port information tables (PITs) on each PE that map customer port indices (CPIs) to provider port indices (PPIs). When a new customer edge device is added, the PE creates or updates a PIT associating that CE with its L1VPN membership. Remote PEs learn about new CEs through manual configuration or automated discovery mechanisms (RFC 5195 using BGP, or RFC 5252 using OSPF).
sections.eli5: A provider might have fiber connections from many different companies, each using different types of circuits. GMPLS works with all of them. When a new customer connects, the provider writes down which customer port connects to which provider port, and tells all the other edge equipment about it.

sections.title: Customer and Provider Control
sections.content:
In L1VPN Basic Mode, the provider controls the PE-to-PE segment (the path across the provider's network) and the customer controls the topology (which of its sites connect to which other sites). A customer can request connections, specify protection requirements, and in some cases choose which PE-to-PE link to use if the customer has multi-homed access. However, the customer cannot control the path inside the provider network or see the provider's internal addresses.

The customer's control is limited to requesting setup, deletion, or modification of L1VPN connections using GMPLS signaling from RFC 5251. The provider network enforces connectivity restrictions based on policy, ensuring that each L1VPN connection only links CEs belonging to the same customer's L1VPN, preventing accidental cross-connection to other customers.
sections.eli5: The customer is like a tenant saying 'I want my Boston office to reach my New York office.' The provider is like a landlord who decides which cables carry that connection, how they are protected if a cable breaks, and what the bill is. The customer cannot see inside the landlord's wiring.

sections.title: Security, Scalability, and Resiliency
sections.content:
Basic Mode L1VPN provides strong topology confidentiality: the customer cannot learn about the provider's network topology or other customers' topologies. The provider protects against external control by validating L1VPN membership and refusing signaling requests from unknown CEs. Data plane security benefits from the inherent difficulty of intercepting optical signals. Control plane security requires authentication of CE-to-PE relationships and optionally encryption of control messages using RSVP-TE integrity objects or IPsec tunnels.

Scalability is bounded by the number of L1VPNs and CE-to-PE links the PE can support; implementations may impose limits. Data plane resiliency supports PE-to-PE segment recovery and CE-to-PE link protection. Control plane resiliency uses GMPLS mechanisms like LMP for control channel management and RSVP-TE graceful restart. Multi-homing for customer resiliency (using multiple PEs) is not supported in Basic Mode, as that would require routing information exchange with the customer.
sections.eli5: The provider keeps its internal network secret from customers. Bad guys cannot wire-tap optical signals easily. If a link breaks, the network can reroute automatically. Very big providers might run out of space for more L1VPNs, but that is uncommon.
